component_checks.metering_device.nodes.c: The capillary tube has ruptured — full loss of refrigerant charge. Replace the tube, find the root cause (vibration, corrosion), and do a full recharge by weight per the nameplate.
The capillary tube is kinked/bent — a mechanical restriction on refrigerant flow. Check the tube's routing and straighten it out; replace the tube if the damage isn't reversible.
Oil residue in atypical spots (leak indicator)
Oil residue in atypical spots around the capillary tube — a characteristic leak indicator, not just dirt. Use an electronic leak detector or UV dye to pinpoint it before topping off.
Capillary tube is OK. Continue with the intake checklist.
Partial restriction in the capillary tube (debris, wax, ice) — check the filter-drier upstream of the tube; replace both the tube and the drier if needed, and flush the circuit.
Suspected wrong capillary tube sizing after a compressor swap — a diameter/length mismatch gives incorrect metering. Check the manufacturer's spec for the installed compressor.
component_checks.metering_device.nodes.e: The control board isn't sending a correct drive signal to the valve (open circuit, wrong polarity, bad driver) — check the wiring and the board's output signals against the schematic.
The valve won't find its home (reference) position during calibration — check the init procedure per the manufacturer's docs, and the coil's connector/wiring.
Mechanical jam on the valve stem (debris, corrosion, deformation) — the valve can't change its opening regardless of the drive signal. The valve needs to be disassembled/replaced.
Bad signal from the control board
Oil residue in atypical spots (leak indicator)
Oil residue in atypical spots around the EEV — a characteristic leak indicator, not just dirt. Use an electronic leak detector or UV dye to pinpoint it before topping off.
EEV is OK. Continue with the intake checklist.
Condition of the EEV (electronic expansion valve)?
The valve's stepper motor sticks/skips steps — the valve doesn't track commands accurately. Check the motor windings and the stem's mechanical freedom of movement.
component_checks.metering_device.nodes.n: No metering device installed or identified on this equipment.
component_checks.metering_device.nodes.o: The piston is clogged with debris/copper oxide — restricting refrigerant flow. Clean or replace the piston, check the filter-drier, and flush the circuit clean after the repair.
Bore erosion/wear on the piston — the enlarged opening passes more refrigerant than designed, which can look like low superheat symptoms. Replace the piston.
Oil residue in atypical spots (leak indicator)
Oil residue in atypical spots around the piston/distributor — a characteristic leak indicator, not just dirt. Use an electronic leak detector or UV dye to pinpoint it before topping off.
Fixed orifice/piston is OK. Continue with the intake checklist.
Condition of the fixed orifice / piston?
Suspected wrong piston size (bore diameter doesn't match the unit's capacity) — check the manufacturer's spec.
component_checks.metering_device.nodes.s: Is a metering device installed on this equipment?
component_checks.metering_device.nodes.t: The TXV's remote bulb lost its charge or came loose from the suction line — the valve stops responding to superheat and can stick in one position. Replace the power element/bulb assembly.

The bulb is mounted with poor thermal contact (wrong clock position, no thermal paste/strap, not insulated from ambient air) — gives false superheat readings. Remount the bulb per the manufacturer's spec.
The power element's diaphragm is damaged — the valve loses its ability to modulate. Replace the power element/TXV assembly.
Internal leak-by through the valve (won't fully close) — elevated suction pressure and low superheat even at light load. Replace the valve.
Oil residue in atypical spots (leak indicator)
The valve is oil-logged — stuck in one position from oil/varnish contamination. Check the system's oil quality/quantity and the compressor's overall condition.
Oil residue in atypical spots around the TXV — a characteristic leak indicator, not just dirt. Use an electronic leak detector or UV dye to pinpoint it before topping off.
TXV is OK. Continue with the intake checklist.

nodes.gas_fault_code.text: Describe the fault code / the number and pattern of the LED flashes, plus the equipment model — I'll pass this to the AI assistant to decode it and give recommendations.
nodes.gas_flame_sensor.related_checks[0]: Measure the actual ionization signal with a microammeter, not just a visual inspection of the sensor
nodes.gas_flame_sensor.related_checks[1]: Check the heat exchanger near the sensor for soot/cracks — can distort the signal
nodes.gas_flame_sensor.text: Classic case — a dirty/worn flame sensor (ionization rod), or poor burner grounding. Also check line-voltage polarity (hot/neutral) — reversed polarity can interfere with the ionization signal — and inlet gas pressure.
nodes.gas_ignition.options[0].label: Nothing at all, the blower doesn't start
nodes.gas_ignition.options[1].label: Spark/flame occurs but drops out (flame-sensor lockout)
nodes.gas_ignition.options[2].label: The control board is flashing a fault code
nodes.gas_ignition.text: What happens when it tries to ignite?
nodes.gas_lights_no_heat.text: Burner lights but heat output is low: check for cold-air infiltration in the return duct, the high-limit switch, the heat exchanger for blockage/cracks (important for CO safety!), manifold gas pressure, and the gas valve setting.
nodes.gas_no_power.text: Check: power/breaker, whether the 'call for heat' signal is reaching the board from the thermostat, the high-limit switch, the door interlock (on some models), and the control-board fuse.
nodes.gas_start.options[0].label: Yes, it lights, but little/no heat
nodes.gas_start.options[1].label: No ignition
nodes.hp_cond_clear.options[0].label: Yes, full speed
nodes.hp_cond_clear.options[1].label: No, running slow/not turning
nodes.hp_cond_clear.text: Are the condenser fan(s) running at full rated speed?
nodes.hp_dirty_cond.text: A dirty/restricted condenser coil is the leading cause of high head pressure. Clean the coil, check air clearances (no hot-air recirculation), and fan direction and speed.
nodes.hp_fan_issue.text: The condenser fan isn't reaching full speed — check the motor, the run capacitor, the control board/signal for EC motors, the fan-speed staging relay, phasing, and the condition of the fan blade.
nodes.hp_fans_ok.options[0].label: High subcooling
nodes.hp_fans_ok.options[1].label: Normal/low subcooling with high pressure
nodes.hp_noncond_refrigerant.text: What refrigerant is in the system?
nodes.hp_noncondensables.related_checks[: Check the evacuation history from the last time the circuit was serviced (depth/duration)
If a sight glass is installed, check for bubbles/moisture
nodes.hp_noncondensables.text: Non-condensable gases (air/nitrogen) in the circuit raise pressure above what the refrigerant alone would show at rest at that temperature. If the standing pressure test came back elevated — recovery, evacuation, and a full recharge by weight resolve it; if the pressure was normal, look elsewhere for the high-pressure cause (dirty condenser, restricted filter, overcharge, etc.).
nodes.hp_overcharge.checklist[0].label: Charging history/records reviewed
nodes.hp_overcharge.checklist[1].label: Line set length/diameter recalculated
nodes.hp_overcharge.checklist[2].label: Refrigerant recovered (weight)
nodes.hp_overcharge.checklist[3].label: Subcooling after adjustment
nodes.hp_overcharge.related_checks[0]: Check condenser condition (dirty/blocked fins) — this also raises head pressure
nodes.hp_overcharge.related_checks[1]: Check condenser fan operation (speed, rotation direction)
nodes.hp_overcharge.text: High subcooling with high head pressure = overcharge. Check the charging history and the weight calculation (the line set may have been charged for a nominal rather than actual length/diameter). Recover the excess through the service port, accounting for ambient conditions and the manufacturer's target subcooling/superheat.
nodes.hp_standing_calc.text: Calculation: comparison against expected saturation pressure
nodes.hp_standing_temp.text: Equipment/ambient temperature at the point of the standing pressure test
nodes.hp_start.options[0].label: Yes, dirty/restricted
nodes.hp_start.options[1].label: No, clean and unrestricted
nodes.hp_start.text: Is the condenser coil (outdoor air-cooled coil) dirty or airflow-restricted?
nodes.ice_overcool.text: Ice with an overcooled space usually means the thermostat/sensor isn't shutting the compressor off in time, or the defrost timer/relay is faulty. Check the thermostat settings and the return-air temperature sensor.
nodes.ice_start.options[0].label: Below normal (overcooled)
nodes.ice_start.options[1].label: Above normal, despite ice
nodes.ice_start.text: With ice present, what's the space/box temperature:
nodes.ice_undercool.checklist[0].label: Airflow checked (filter/blower)
nodes.ice_undercool.checklist[1].label: Charge checked for undercharge
nodes.ice_undercool.checklist[2].label: Defrost cycle checked (timer/sensor/heaters) — refrigeration equipment/heat pumps
nodes.ice_undercool.checklist[3].label: Condensate pan/drain heater checked, if fitted — RTU/AC units with no defrost cycle
nodes.ice_undercool.checklist[4].label: Liquid-line solenoid checked
nodes.ice_undercool.related_checks[0]: Check door/gasket seals on refrigeration equipment (moist-air infiltration accelerates icing)
nodes.ice_undercool.related_checks[1]: Check the evaporator fins for internal buildup, not just the external filter
nodes.ice_undercool.text: Ice with insufficient cooling is almost always low airflow (filter/blower) or an undercharge. For refrigeration equipment, also check the defrost cycle: the timer, defrost-termination sensor, defrost heaters, and the liquid-line solenoid.
nodes.leak_condensate.options[0].label: Yes, checked — clear
nodes.leak_condensate.options[1].label: No, not checked yet
nodes.leak_condensate.text: Has the drain line and trap been checked for a clog?
nodes.leak_condensate_clear.text: Drain is clear but the leak continues — check for a crack in the drain pan, correct P-trap height (an undersized trap under strong exhaust suction can siphon water back), line insulation, and excess condensation from oversized airflow.
nodes.leak_condensate_clog.text: A clogged drain line/trap is the most common cause. Clear the line (nitrogen/vacuum purge), check the pipe slope, condensate pump operation (if fitted), and the float switch.
nodes.leak_refrig.checklist[0].label: Leak located (electronic detector/UV dye)
nodes.leak_refrig.checklist[1].label: Leak location
nodes.leak_refrig.checklist[2].label: Leak repaired before recharging
nodes.leak_refrig.checklist[3].label: Full recharge by weight per nameplate
nodes.leak_refrig.related_checks[0]: Inspect brazed joints for flux residue/oxidation — a common source of hidden leaks
nodes.leak_refrig.related_checks[1]: Check the equipment's history for prior leaks/repairs
nodes.leak_refrig.text: Signs of a refrigerant leak — oil residue in atypical spots (fittings, tubing bends, around brazed joints) is a reliable leak indicator, not just dirt. Use an electronic leak detector or UV dye to pinpoint it exactly. Don't top off 'by feel' before repairing — find and fix the leak first, then do a full recharge by weight per the nameplate.
nodes.leak_start.options[0].label: Condensate drainage
nodes.leak_start.options[1].label: Looks like a refrigerant leak (oil residue in atypical spots)
nodes.leak_start.options[2].label: Other
nodes.leak_start.text: Is this condensate drainage or does it look like a refrigerant circuit leak?
nodes.lp_airflow_bad.text: Insufficient airflow across the evaporator is the most common cause of low-pressure trips and subsequent freeze-ups. Replace/clean the filter, check the coil for blockage, the blower/belt, ductwork, and damper positions.
nodes.lp_airflow_ok.options[0].label: Yes, low subcooling
nodes.lp_airflow_ok.options[1].label: No, subcooling is normal
nodes.lp_metering.text: Airflow is fine, subcooling isn't low, but suction is still low — check the metering device (TXV/cap tube) for a partial restriction (moisture, ice, debris inside) and the TXV's superheat setting (over-tightened = closing more than it should).
nodes.lp_rapid_trip_result_receiver.rela: King valve on the liquid line — fully open?
Do the LP switch settings (cut-in/cut-out/differential) match the equipment's spec?
Oil traces in unusual places — a sign of a leak, and a leak produces the same rapid LP-trip picture
nodes.lp_rapid_trip_result_receiver.text: The safety trips before the pressure can stabilize, so any superheat/subcooling reading taken now is physically unreliable — don't build on it. On a system with a receiver, first confirm liquid is reaching the evaporator at all: the king/queen valve on the liquid line (partially closed after the last service?), the liquid-line solenoid, the filter-drier's temperature drop, and the feed through the metering device. Separately, check the LP switch settings themselves: unlike an RTU, this class of equipment usually has adjustable switches, and cut-in/cut-out/differential may have been set away from spec.
nodes.lp_rapid_trip_result_rtu.related_c: LP/HP switches on an RTU are usually factory-set and brazed into the circuit: if the calibration has drifted, that's a switch replacement, not a field adjustment
Metering device (TXV or piston) — icing/frost at the inlet, temperature drop across the filter-drier
Oil traces in unusual places — a sign of a leak, and a leak produces the same rapid LP-trip picture
nodes.lp_rapid_trip_result_rtu.text: The safety trips before the pressure can stabilize, which means any superheat/subcooling reading taken now is physically unreliable — don't build on it. First work out why the pressure collapses on start-up: liquid feed to the evaporator (TXV or piston/fixed orifice — partial restriction, icing, a plugged filter-drier ahead of it), the actual charge (a leak produces exactly this picture), and the LP switch itself, which may have drifted out of calibration or be sticking. Note: without a receiver, there's no king/queen valve to check — 'is the king valve open' doesn't apply here, there's nothing there to find.

nodes.lp_receiver_check.options[1].label: No receiver on this system
nodes.lp_receiver_check.text: Does this system have a receiver (liquid line, with a king/queen valve)?

nodes.lp_stable_check.text: Does the compressor run long enough for the readings to stabilize, or does the low-pressure safety trip it almost immediately (short-cycling)?
nodes.lp_start.options[0].label: Yes, airflow is fine
nodes.lp_start.options[1].label: No, restricted/dirty filter

nodes.nc_lowsuction_okSC.text: Low suction with normal subcooling most often points to insufficient evaporator airflow — check the filter, the indoor blower, and air distribution.
nodes.nc_no_condfan.text: Condenser fan isn't running while the compressor is on — this quickly drives up head pressure. Check the motor run capacitor, windings, the fan control board/relay, and the motor fuse. Don't delay — the high-pressure switch will trip.
nodes.nc_pressures_ok.text: Pressures are roughly normal but cooling is still insufficient. Describe additional details (supply air temperature, evaporator ΔT, compressor amp draw, service history) — this will help the AI assistant give a precise analysis.
nodes.nc_refrigerant.text: What refrigerant is in the system?

nodes.nc_running.options[1].label: No, not spinning / spinning slowly

nodes.nc_sc_high.checklist[0].label: Filter-drier inspected for cold spot/pressure drop
nodes.nc_sc_high.checklist[1].label: Liquid line checked for kinks/pinches
nodes.nc_sc_high.checklist[2].label: Filter-drier replaced
nodes.nc_sc_high.related_checks[0]: Check the temperature drop across each liquid-line component individually, if present (solenoid, sight glass, TXV — a basic RTU may have neither a solenoid nor a sight glass)
nodes.nc_sc_high.related_checks[1]: Inspect the full line length for physical damage, not just around the filter-drier
nodes.nc_sc_high.text: Low suction with high subcooling points to a restriction on the liquid line — a clogged filter-drier, a kinked line, or a partially closed valve. Tell-tale sign: a cold spot/temperature drop across the filter-drier. Replace the drier and check the line for kinks or pinches.
nodes.nc_sc_low.checklist[0].label: Leak search performed (electronic detector / bubble test)
nodes.nc_sc_low.checklist[1].label: Leak location found
nodes.nc_sc_low.checklist[2].label: Leak repaired
nodes.nc_sc_low.checklist[3].label: Recharge weight added
nodes.nc_sc_low.related_checks[0]: Check service history for prior leaks in the same area of the circuit
nodes.nc_sc_low.related_checks[1]: If a moisture/liquid indicator is installed, check its condition (wet/bubbling)
nodes.nc_sc_low.text: Low suction + low subcooling = undercharge or a leak. Find the leak (electronic leak detector / bubble test on fittings), repair it, then recharge by weight — not 'by feel' on the gauges.
nodes.nc_sh_high.checklist[0].label: Checked evaporator airflow (filter, blower, coil)
nodes.nc_sh_high.checklist[1].label: Verified TXV operation (bulb, equalizer line)
nodes.nc_sh_high.checklist[2].label: Measured subcooling
nodes.nc_sh_high.checklist[3].label: Ruled out undercharge via subcooling reading
nodes.nc_sh_high.related_checks[0]: Check refrigerant distribution across the evaporator tubes (distributor not clogged)
nodes.nc_sh_high.related_checks[1]: Compare the measured superheat against the manufacturer's target for this metering-device type
nodes.nc_sh_high.text: High suction + high superheat — insufficient flow through the TXV/cap tube under a heavy load, a TXV that isn't opening enough, or a noticeable undercharge combined with high load. Check the evaporator's air-side load, TXV operation, and liquid-line subcooling.
nodes.nc_sh_low_highsuction.checklist[3]: Compressor checked for floodback/oil dilution signs
nodes.nc_sh_low_highsuction.related_chec: Check compressor oil level and color (signs of dilution from floodback)
Check that the crankcase heater is functioning
nodes.nc_sh_low_highsuction.text: High suction with low superheat — risk of evaporator overfeeding and compressor floodback. Check whether the TXV is stuck open, whether the system is overcharged, the condition of the TXV sensing bulb/element, and the bulb's insulation.

nodes.nc_start.options[1].label: No, it doesn't start

nodes.nc_suction_low.text: Is there ice on the evaporator or the suction line?
nodes.nh_electric_result.text: Check: breakers/fuses on the heat-strip circuit, high-limit switch trip, element continuity (resistance check), sequencer / stage-heat relay operation, and airflow (strips often trip the limit when airflow is low).
nodes.nh_hp_2.options[0].label: Yes, normal
nodes.nh_hp_2.options[1].label: No, high pressure
nodes.nh_hp_2.options[2].label: No, low pressure
nodes.nh_hp_2.text: Do heating-mode pressures match the P-T chart for the current condensing/evaporating temperature?
nodes.nh_hp_novalve.text: Looks like a reversing valve problem (stuck mechanically) or a bad solenoid coil (no power / burned out). Check voltage at the coil and the temperature split across the valve ports.
nodes.nh_hp_ok.text: Pressures are normal but heat output is insufficient — check: ice on the outdoor coil (defrost cycle), crankcase heater operation, indoor-unit airflow, thermostat setpoints, and the heat pump's low-ambient lockout logic (auxiliary/emergency heat lockout).
nodes.nh_hp_start.options[0].label: Yes, it shifts
nodes.nh_hp_start.options[1].label: No, it doesn't shift
nodes.nh_hp_start.text: Does the reversing valve shift? (you should hear a click when switching cooling/heating)

nodes.nh_type.options[1].label: Gas heat
nodes.nh_type.options[2].label: Electric heat strips
nodes.nh_type.text: What type of heat does this unit have?
nodes.noise_compressor.text: A metallic knock/valve clatter can indicate floodback (liquid refrigerant returning to the compressor) — check superheat at the compressor inlet. Humming without turning — see the 'won't start' branch. A whining sound from worn bearings on older compressors — consider replacement.
nodes.noise_fan.text: Check fan-blade balance (bent blades), motor bearings (shaft play), the blade's mounting on the shaft, and contact with the fan shroud.
nodes.noise_start.options[0].label: Compressor
nodes.noise_start.options[1].label: Fan (outdoor/indoor)
nodes.noise_start.options[2].label: General vibration/cabinet rattle
nodes.noise_vibration.text: Check the unit's vibration isolators/mounts, roof-curb/frame attachment (for RTUs — curb-adaptor sealing), and compressor mounting bolts inside the unit (transport bolts are sometimes left in during installation — causing resonance).

nodes.ws_amp_logged.text: Compressor current has been logged to the checklist history. If it's within RLA, that's additional confirmation of a healthy start. If it's above RLA, see the flag above in the history — that alone isn't a verdict on the compressor, but does call for weighing the bigger picture (age, failure history, vibration, noise) before deciding on replacement.
nodes.ws_amp_measurement.reference.label: Nameplate RLA (compressor data plate)

nodes.ws_contactor_bad.text: 24V is present but the contactor won't pull in — the contactor itself is bad (burned coil or stuck/welded contacts). Replace the contactor.
nodes.ws_contactor_no.options[0].label: Yes, 24V present
nodes.ws_contactor_no.options[1].label: No 24V
nodes.ws_contactor_no.text: Is there 24V at the contactor coil on a call?
nodes.ws_contactor_pulls.options[0].labe: Hums but doesn't turn (locked rotor / hard start)
nodes.ws_contactor_pulls.text: What does the compressor do once the contactor pulls in?
nodes.ws_control_circuit.text: No 24V at the coil — look for an open in the control circuit: safety switches (high/low pressure, freeze stat, condensate float switch, door/access interlock), the transformer fuse, and the thermostat and its wiring.
nodes.ws_locked_rotor.checklist[0].label: Start/run capacitor tested
nodes.ws_locked_rotor.checklist[1].label: Winding resistance (megger to ground)
nodes.ws_locked_rotor.checklist[2].label: Start-up voltage sag checked

nodes.ws_locked_rotor.related_checks[0]: Check the history of overload/compressor-protector trips
nodes.ws_locked_rotor.related_checks[1]: If insulation breakdown is suspected, megger-test the windings at elevated voltage
nodes.ws_locked_rotor.text: Signs of a locked rotor: check the start/run capacitor, compressor winding resistance (short to ground/open winding), and voltage sag at start-up. If the capacitor and windings check out, a mechanically seized compressor is likely — replacement is needed.
nodes.ws_no_load.text: The contactor clicks but there's no load current — check the contactor's load-side terminals, fuses/breaker downstream of the contactor, and the compressor windings for an open.
nodes.ws_no_power.text: No incoming power — check the panel breaker/fuses, the disconnect switch near the unit, wiring and terminal integrity (burned connections), and power to the control transformer (24V), if applicable.
